Authorities identified the shooter as 22-year-old Matti Juhani Saari, who unleashed gunfire inside a classroom at the School of Hospitality in Kauhajoki before turning the weapon on himself. Approximately 150 students were on campus at the time of the attack. Jukka Forsberg, a maintenance worker at the institution, told YLE that the perpetrator was wearing a ski mask and carrying a large bag when he entered the building. 

"I heard several dozen rounds of shots. In other words, it was an automatic pistol," Forsberg said. "I saw some female students who were wailing and moaning, and one managed to escape out the back door."

Plumes of smoke were seen billowing from a campus building, though officials were initially unable to determine the cause of the fire. 

Tapio Varmola, who was visiting the school during the attack, told CNN he was in a nearby building roughly two blocks away when the shooting began. In the immediate aftermath, he recalled hearing frantic cries from fleeing students. Varmola noted that emergency personnel arrived approximately 10 minutes after receiving the call, adding, "It took two hours to get this situation ended."

Saari died Tuesday afternoon at Tampere University Hospital from a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head, confirmed Medical Director Matti Lehto. Lehto added that at least one other individual sustained severe injuries during the assault.

Law enforcement revealed that police had questioned and subsequently released Saari just a day prior, on Monday, after discovering violent videos he had uploaded to YouTube. National Police Commissioner Mikko Paatero informed YLE that because Saari had made no explicit threats in the recordings, there were no legal grounds to detain him. Authorities were first alerted to the videos on Friday but were unable to locate Saari until Monday, at which point officers also conducted a search of his residence.

According to the suspect's YouTube profile, four videos posted under the username "Mr. Saari" from Kauhajoki depicted a man discharging a handgun at a shooting range. The profile also featured a video tribute to the Columbine High School perpetrators, Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold, placed at the top of his favorites list. The municipality of Kauhajoki, home to roughly 15,000 residents, lies approximately 290 kilometers (180 miles) northwest of the capital, Helsinki.

"All these memories are being brought back and people are asking the question, 'Why again?'" Sipila reflected.

**KAUHAJOKI, Finland (CNN)** — In a horrific replay of a tragedy that shocked the nation less than a year prior, a gunman opened fire at a vocational college in western Finland on Tuesday, killing 10 people and setting off fires before turning the gun on himself, authorities said. 

The massacre at the Seinäjoki University of Applied Sciences campus in Kauhajoki, a quiet town roughly 180 miles (290 kilometers) northwest of the capital, Helsinki, has left the Nordic country in deep mourning and reignited a fierce national debate over its deeply rooted gun culture.

The shooter was identified by police as Matti Juhani Saari, a 22-year-old culinary arts student at the school. Wearing a ski mask and armed with a semi-automatic Walther .22-caliber pistol, Saari entered a classroom around 11:00 a.m. local time where roughly 20 students were taking an exam. 

According to police, Saari fired repeatedly into the crowd of students, left the room to ignite several homemade firebombs, and continued shooting in the corridors. He later shot himself in the head as police surrounded the building. He was rushed to Tampere University Hospital, where he died of his injuries several hours later.

All 10 victims—nine students and one teacher—died at the scene. Police said the vast majority of the dead were women in their early 20s.

### 'Panic broke out instantly'

Survivors recounted moments of absolute terror as shots echoed through the concrete halls of the school. 

"We heard loud bangs, but at first we thought someone had dropped a heavy table or that it was construction work," said Jukka Forsberg, a maintenance worker at the school who was near the classroom when the shooting began. "Then I saw a young man walking down the corridor with a large gun bag. Seconds later, people started screaming and running out of the room. Panic broke out instantly."

Students fled into the surrounding fields in sub-zero temperatures, while others jumped from second-story windows to escape the gunfire and rising smoke. 

"I saw students crying, covered in soot, throwing themselves out of shattered windows," said 21-year-old student Hanna Tuominen, who was in an adjacent wing of the building when the alarms sounded. "You never think something like this could happen in a town where everyone knows everyone. It felt like a nightmare."

### Police under scrutiny over missed warning signs

The massacre triggered immediate public outrage after law enforcement officials revealed that Saari had been interviewed by police just 24 hours before the attack—and allowed to keep his weapon.

Police had questioned Saari on Monday regarding several videos he had posted to YouTube. In the clips, uploaded under the username "W.R.08," Saari was seen firing a handgun at a shooting range, accompanied by unsettling messages, including one that read: "You will die next."

Despite the ominous postings, officers concluded that Saari did not pose an immediate threat and lacked legal grounds to confiscate his weapon or revoke his permit, which he had legally obtained just six weeks earlier.

"The shooter was interviewed by police on Monday regarding the videos found online," Finnish Interior Minister Anne Holmlund said at a press conference in Helsinki. "However, the detective in charge decided at the time that there was no reason to revoke his gun license. A full investigation into the actions of the police department involved has been launched."

Police Chief Superintendent Jari Neulaniemi defended the initial response while acknowledging the tragic outcome. "At the time of the interview, the suspect presented himself calmly and co-operatively," Neulaniemi said. "Based on the strict legal threshold required to seize property at the time, the interviewing officer made a judgment call. Naturally, in light of today's terrible events, that decision will be thoroughly re-examined."

Investigating officers later searched Saari’s dormitory room, discovering handwritten notes left behind that explicitly outlined his intention to commit a mass murder. "The target was the school, the weapon was a pistol, and the motivation was a deep hatred for humanity," lead investigator Tapio Varmola told reporters.

### Echoes of Jokela and Finland's gun culture

The Kauhajoki shooting bears striking similarities to the Jokela High School massacre in November 2007, when 18-year-old Pekka-Eric Auvinen shot and killed eight people before taking his own life. Like Saari, Auvinen was a young man who posted warning videos on YouTube, used a legally acquired .22-caliber pistol, and targeted his own educational institution.

The two back-to-back tragedies have turned an intense global spotlight on Finland's gun laws. 

Despite its reputation as one of the safest and most peaceful nations in the world, Finland ranks among the top countries globally in per-capita gun ownership, driven by deeply entrenched traditions of hunting and target shooting. With a population of roughly 5.3 million people at the time, Finland had more than 1.6 million registered firearms in circulation.

Under existing Finnish law, citizens as young as 15 could legally own firearms with parental consent, and handguns could be acquired for target practice without a rigorous mental health evaluation. 

In the wake of Tuesday’s attack, Finnish Prime Minister Matti Vanhanen signaled that systemic changes to the country's firearm laws were now inevitable.

"We must ask ourselves how it is possible that young people can gain access to weapons like this so easily," Vanhanen told reporters after visiting the scene in Kauhajoki. "It is time for us to seriously consider whether private individuals should be permitted to own handguns at all."

### A nation in mourning

By Tuesday evening, hundreds of local residents gathered at Kauhajoki’s main church to light candles and lay flowers in the snow. Flags across the country were ordered to fly at half-mast, and a national day of mourning was declared for Wednesday.

For the small community of Kauhajoki, the road to recovery will be long and painful.

"Our town is broken," said Mayor Antti Rantakangas. "We are a tight-knit community, and almost everyone here knows a family affected by this unspeakable act. Tonight, we weep for our children."

**KAUHAJOKI, Finland** — In a tragedy that has sent shockwaves across Scandinavia, a 22-year-old student opened fire at a vocational college in western Finland on Tuesday, killing ten people before turning the gun on himself. 

The attack at the Seinäjoki University of Applied Sciences in Kauhajoki is the second deadly school shooting in Finland in less than a year. However, growing outrage is now turning toward law enforcement after officials confirmed that police had questioned the gunman just 24 hours before the massacre regarding threatening videos he posted on YouTube—and allowed him to keep his firearm.

### The Attack

The gunman, identified as culinary arts student Matti Juhani Saari, entered the school shortly before 11:00 a.m. local time, wearing a ski mask and dressed in black. Armed with a .22-caliber semi-automatic Walther P22 target pistol and several improvised petrol bombs, Saari stormed a classroom where a group of second-year students was taking an exam.

Witnesses described scenes of panic as gunshots echoed through the corridors. Saari fired repeatedly at students and teachers at point-blank range and set fire to the classroom using incendiary devices, severely burning several bodies and complicating early identification efforts. 

Emergency services responded rapidly, surrounding the building. After a standoff lasting nearly two hours, during which Saari set further fires and fired shots at responding officers, the gunman turned the weapon on himself, shooting himself in the head. He died hours later at Tampere University Hospital.

In total, nine students—eight females and one male—and one male teacher were killed. One other student sustained gunshot wounds but is reported to be in stable condition.

### The YouTube Trail

As investigators work to establish a clear motive, a chilling digital footprint left behind by Saari has come to light. Under the online moniker "WAF42," Saari had uploaded dozens of videos to the file-sharing website YouTube in the weeks leading up to the attack.

In several of the clips, Saari is seen wearing dark clothing, pointing a handgun directly at the camera, and firing multiple rounds at a local shooting range. One video was posted with the caption: *"You will die next."* 

In another clip, shot just days before the attack, Saari addresses the camera directly, saying, *"Life is a special offer, but death is for free,"* before firing four shots toward the lens. 

Saari’s YouTube profile also included references to the 1999 Columbine High School massacre in the United States, listing his interests as "guns, computers, sex, and beer," and citing his favorite song as "You Know You're Right" by Nirvana.

### Police Questioned Shooter 24 Hours Prior

The revelation of Saari's social media activity has placed Finnish authorities under intense scrutiny. During a press conference Tuesday evening, Finnish Interior Minister Anne Holmlund confirmed that local police had been alerted to Saari’s YouTube videos by concerned citizens over the weekend.

On Monday—just one day before the shooting—detectives called Saari in for questioning regarding the disturbing uploads. 

However, after interviewing the 22-year-old, officers concluded there was no legal ground to detain him or confiscate his weapon. Saari had held a temporary permit for the .22-caliber pistol, legally obtained in August 2008. 

"The police officer who interviewed him decided that there was no reason to revoke his gun license," Minister Holmlund told reporters. "We must now investigate fully why that decision was made and whether proper protocols were followed."

National Police Commissioner Mikko Paatero acknowledged the mounting public criticism, stating that an internal investigation had been launched to determine why the firearm was left in Saari’s possession despite the clear red flags raised by his online behavior.

### A Nation in Shock and Demands for Reform

The Kauhajoki shooting bears horrifying similarities to the Jokela High School massacre of November 2007, in which 18-year-old Pekka-Eric Auvinen killed eight people after posting warning videos on YouTube under the handle "Sturmgeist89." 

The striking parallels between the two incidents have reignited a fierce national debate over Finland's gun laws. Despite its low crime rate, Finland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the world per capita, deeply rooted in a strong hunting culture.

Prime Minister Matti Vanhanen, who declared Wednesday a national day of mourning, indicated that strict legislative action is now inevitable. 

"It is time to consider whether private individuals should have access to handguns at all," Vanhanen said after visiting the site of the shooting. "We must ask ourselves how a tragedy like this could happen again so soon."
